title: Finite-presentation invariant open pieces of a flat group sheaf over a trait
statement: Let $R$ be a strictly henselian discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring, def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], meaning a henselian local ring with separably closed residue field, $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$, and $F$ an fpqc sheaf of groups on $S$-schemes. A group sheaf takes values in groups, not necessarily commutative. A group scheme has multiplication, identity and inverse morphisms satisfying the group identities. An fpqc sheaf means a contravariant set-valued functor on $S$-schemes satisfying the covering equalizer condition of [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering]. Suppose an fpqc morphism $p:T\to S$ makes $F_T$ representable as a group sheaf by a separated flat $T$-group scheme $P$ locally of finite presentation. Flatness is [def-weil-flat-morphism]; separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. There exist an open subgroup subfunctor $H\subseteq F$ and a set-indexed covering family of $H$-invariant open subfunctors $(U_a\subseteq F)_{a\in A}$ [def-pc-subfunctor]. Open means that for every scheme $V$ and section in $F(V)$ the inverse image subfunctor is represented by an open subscheme of $V$ [def-weil-open-immersion]; covering means that these opens cover every such $V$. The sheaves $H_T$ and $(U_a)_T$ are represented by separated flat schemes of finite presentation over $T$. For each $a$ there is a finite field extension $L_a/K$, where $K$ is the fraction field of $R$, such that, writing $R_a$ for the integral closure of $R$ in $L_a$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] and $B_a=\operatorname{Spec}R_a$, the canonical morphism $b_a:B_a\to S$ is integral [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], surjective, flat and quasi-compact, hence fpqc, and has finite underlying fibres. The extension may be ramified; no etaleness or finiteness of $R_a$ as an $R$-module is required. The scheme $B_a$ is a semi-trait: its ring is a domain with finitely many maximal ideals, Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] and normal [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], of dimension one (strict prime-ideal chains have length at most one and some chain has length one). Over $B_a$, $(U_a)_{B_a}$ is a finite union of $H_{B_a}$-invariant open subfunctors $V_{aj}$ for which $(h,x)\mapsto(hx,x)$ from $H_{B_a}\times_{B_a}V_{aj}$ to $V_{aj}\times_{B_a}V_{aj}$ is surjective as a morphism of fppf sheaves [def-pc-fppf-site]. This local-lifting description persists after every further base change. No representability of $F$, $H$, or $U_a$ over $S$ is asserted.

source.place: Lemma 4.2.4 and its following action argument, printed pp.59-61 (4.2 Step 5), for the subgroup and special-fibre component pieces. Agent extension for generic-only pieces: finite Galois-stable unions of generic H-cosets split over a finite field extension; replace finite etale covers by normalization in a finite possibly ramified extension. Source field case 4.1 and normalization argument 4.2.1 supply the field and normalization inputs. This is invariant-open structure, not representability on S. Repair of E2 at returned head 1373c1175ce; full justification and ramified lattice test in report.md. Local archive WANTED; primary scan https://www.numdam.org/article/MSMF_1973__33__5_0.pdf

proof.text: Use the component-envelope lemma, and let $Z_0$ be the identity component of $F_s$. Put $H=E_F(Z_0)$. The identity section lies in $H$, and inversion preserves it by isomorphism compatibility. Here $R$ is strictly henselian, so the lemma's corrected neutral-product clause applies and gives $E_{F\times_SF}(Z_0\times_sZ_0)=H\times_SH$. This equality is not used over a nonhenselian DVR. For multiplication $m:F\times_SF\to F$, $(x,y)\mapsto(xy,y)$ is an automorphism with inverse $(z,y)\mapsto(zy^{-1},y)$; hence $m$ is a projection up to this automorphism and is flat and locally finitely presented after the representing cover, by the cited base-change statements. On the special fibre, $m$ maps $Z_0\times_sZ_0$ onto $Z_0$ since $z=m(z,1)$. The envelope lemma's flat-map compatibility now gives $m(H\times_SH)\subset H$. Thus $H$ is an open subgroup, and the envelope lemma gives that $H_T$ is separated flat and of finite presentation. In particular, no subgroup property is inferred merely from existence or minimality of an envelope.

source.place: 4.2 Step 5, printed pp.59-61; agent assembly of cited inputs

proof.text: Apply the coset-space lemma to this $H$. Choose its covering opens $Q_a\subset Q=H\backslash F$ and put $U_a=F\times_Q Q_a$. These are open subfunctors by their scheme-test definition. For a section $x\in F(V)$ the map $V\to Q$ induced by $x$ pulls the covering opens $Q_a$ back to opens covering $V$, so the $U_a$ cover in exactly the sense of the statement. Since $q(hx)=q(x)$, they are $H$-invariant. The sheaf $(U_a)_T$ is represented by the inverse-image open of $Q_{a,T}$ in $P$. The coset lemma gives $q_T$ flat separated and finitely presented; $Q_{a,T}\to T$ is finitely presented by base change. Their composite is finitely presented by the cited composition theorem. This open subscheme of the separated flat $T$-scheme $P$ remains separated and flat, by restricting the diagonal and stalk maps. This proves all the finite-presentation assertions before making any normalization cover.

source.place: 4.2 Step 5, printed pp.59-61; agent assembly of cited inputs

proof.text: Fix $a$. Take the finite affine etale atlas $W_{ai}\to Q_a$ of the coset lemma. Apply the finite-base splitting theorem to the finite family $W_{ai}\to S$. Its hypotheses hold: $S$ is Noetherian, and the atlas pieces are separated etale of finite presentation. We get a finite surjection $C_a\to S$ with $W_{ai}\times_SC_a$ a finite disjoint union of open subschemes of $C_a$. It is essential here that the theorem applies to the separated scheme charts, not that $Q_a\to S$ be separated. These open charts jointly surject onto $Q_a\times_SC_a$.

source.place: Inherited trait descent in proof (3); auxiliary finite etale chart splitting is Orgogozo Lemma 9.1.3, read online, as stated in the cited node

proof.text: Write $C_a=\operatorname{Spec}D_a$, where $D_a$ is a finite $R$-algebra. A point of its nonempty generic fibre corresponds to a prime $\mathfrak p_a\subset D_a$ contracting to zero. Set $L_a=\operatorname{Frac}(D_a/\mathfrak p_a)$; this is a finite extension of $K$ since $(D_a/\mathfrak p_a)\otimes_RK$ is a finite-dimensional domain over $K$, hence a field. Every element $x$ of $D_a/\mathfrak p_a$ is integral over $R$: choose finite module generators, express multiplication by $x$ on them by a matrix over $R$, and apply its monic characteristic polynomial using the adjugate identity; it annihilates all generators and hence $1$. Thus every element is integral, so its inclusion in $L_a$ factors through the integral closure $R_a$ by its definition. Thus $B_a=\operatorname{Spec}R_a$ maps to $C_a$ over $S$. This passage uses no etaleness or module-finiteness of $R_a$.

source.place: Definition of a finite algebra and integral closure; elementary generic component of a finite surjective scheme over a domain

proof.text: Apply the integral-closure Dedekind theorem to $R\subset L_a$: the base is a Noetherian dimension-one domain because it is a DVR: every ideal of a PID is finitely generated, and every nonzero prime is generated by an irreducible and is maximal; the nonzero maximal ideal gives dimension exactly one. It gives that $R_a$ is a Noetherian normal domain of dimension one and that $B_a\to S$ is surjective with finite fibres. All maximal ideals of $R_a$ lie over the maximal ideal of $R$: for an integral extension the contraction of a maximal ideal is maximal (in the quotient, a subring over which a field is integral is a field). Hence the finite closed fibre contains all maximal ideals, so $R_a$ is semilocal. The inclusion $R\subset R_a\subset L_a$ makes $R_a$ torsion free over the PID $R$, so the cited flatness theorem makes it flat. The affine map $B_a\to S$ is quasi-compact, and is integral by the definition of $R_a$. Together with surjectivity it is fpqc. This proves all assertions about the normalization cover, without excellence.

source.place: Tag 09IG (lemma-integral-closure-Dedekind); torsion-free flatness is Tag 0AUW (lemma-dedekind-torsion-free-flat), PID case

proof.text: Pull the split atlas of Step 3 back along $B_a\to C_a$. It gives finitely many maps $s_j:O_j\to Q_{a,B_a}$, with $O_j\subset B_a$ open, jointly surjective. Each is a section over $O_j$ of the etale map $Q_{a,B_a}\to B_a$. A section is a monomorphism; it is etale by the cited chartwise-etale permanence theorem, since both its source and target are etale over $O_j$. The etale-monomorphism theorem makes $s_j$ an open immersion. Define $V_{aj}=F_{B_a}\times_{Q_{B_a}}s_j(O_j)$. They are $H_{B_a}$-invariant open subfunctors and their finite union is $(U_a)_{B_a}$. On $s_j(O_j)\simeq O_j$, the map $V_{aj}\to B_a$ factors through $O_j$, so $V_{aj}\times_{B_a}V_{aj}=V_{aj}\times_{Q_{B_a}}V_{aj}$. Restricting the torsor isomorphism of the coset lemma identifies this last sheaf with $H_{B_a}\times_{B_a}V_{aj}$ by $(h,x)\mapsto(hx,x)$. In particular the required action map is fppf-surjective.

source.place: Tag 05W5 (lemma-etale-universally-injective-open); section maps are etale by Tag 03FV (lemma-etale-permanence); torsor identity is Tag 06PH

proof.text: Finally, the isomorphism in Step 6 is an isomorphism of sheaves defined by multiplication and the projections. Pulling it back to any $B_a$-scheme preserves its inverse and both inverse identities. The pulled-back $V_{aj}$ are again invariant opens and still cover the pulled-back $U_a$, as is checked by inverse images on every scheme test. The pulled-back action maps are therefore still surjective as fppf sheaf maps. No step has asserted representability of $F$, $H$, or $U_a$ on $S$.
